name: The postwar yield peg
headline: When the cost of financing the Treasury constrained monetary policy
analysis: The wartime interest-rate peg committed the Federal Reserve to supporting government securities. Defending a yield could require buying the bonds investors wanted to sell, increasing bank reserves just as the Fed wanted to restrain inflation. The conflict intensified during the Korean War. The March 1951 Treasury–Fed Accord altered the allocation of responsibility for debt management and monetary policy. It was an institutional break, rather than an ordinary rate announcement. In the month of the accord, industrial output was nearly one-fifth above its level a year earlier. That growth rate compares two months and does not measure the effect of the agreement.
test: To study a modern fiscal-financing constraint, identify an actual obligation to defend a yield, the duration supplied by the government and who absorbed it. Heavy issuance on its own does not reproduce the peg.

name: When the dollar bands gave way
headline: Sterling floated nine months before the Deutsche mark joined the European float against the dollar.
analysis: The August 1971 suspension of official dollar-to-gold convertibility left a separate question open. Which exchange rates would central banks still defend? The December Smithsonian settlement reset parities and widened trading margins. Britain announced a sterling float on 23 June 1972. In March 1973 several European currencies began floating together against the dollar while retaining a band among themselves. Markets officially reopened on 19 March. Each step changed a different constraint for a trader hedging a dollar liability.

details.heading: The mark moved more even on a typical day
details.text: From July 1972 to January 1973, sterling’s mean absolute daily move against the dollar was 0.118% and the mark’s was 0.079%. From late March to September 1973, the averages reached 0.204% and 0.600% on the same 128 observation days. For the mark the median rose from 0.063% to 0.369%. Ending the latter window on 22 June, before the late-June mark realignment, gives 0.412% over 62 days. Extending the window to the end of 1974 gives 0.525% over 423 days. Sterling also moved more despite already floating during both periods. A broader change in dollar conditions accompanied the change in the mark’s regime.

details.heading: What the quotes measure
details.text: The series use the New York noon buying rates. Sterling is quoted in dollars per pound. The German quote is inverted so both returns measure local-currency appreciation against the dollar. The chart averages absolute daily log changes over each month. The table uses interior windows and omits the transition crises. Each daily return requires both currencies to be observed on the date and preceding weekday. Friday to Monday is eligible, holidays with missing observations are not bridged, and unchanged quotes remain in the sample. Two large reversing mark moves in March 1972 influence the first window’s mean. Dropping the two returns touching 17 March reduces that mean from 0.181% to 0.129%.

test: A defended spot rate can conceal pressure in reserve losses, forward discounts or overnight rates. A stronger comparison would measure reserve intervention net of valuation and borrowing, as well as forward rates and dealer spreads, on either side of the regime changes. Volatility in the same dollar pair can reflect a change in the exchange-rate rules, in US news, or in dealer liquidity. These window comparisons do not separate those causes.

name: The first oil shock
headline: Prices accelerated as industrial activity turned down
analysis: U.S. consumer prices were already 7.4% higher than a year earlier in September 1973, the month before the oil embargo. In October inflation reached 8.1%, while industrial production stood 7.2% above its year-earlier level. By December 1974 prices were up 12.1% and industrial production was down 8.4% year on year. Higher energy costs squeezed purchasing power and raised production costs at the same time. The pre-embargo reading shows how much inflation preceded that shock.
test: An oil shock is a better analogue when the source of the oil move, the energy intensity of production and the scope for wages and margins to absorb higher costs resemble those of the comparison period. Compare core prices, wage settlements and output by industry before extrapolating headline CPI.

name: The Volcker disinflation
headline: Inflation and unemployment peaked at different points in the disinflation
analysis: The second oil shock was already under way when the FOMC changed its operating procedure on 6 October 1979. It placed more weight on restraining bank reserve growth and accepted wider fluctuations in the federal funds rate. Annual CPI inflation was 12.1% that October and rose further to 14.6% in March 1980. The eventual decline came with substantial real costs. In November 1982 inflation was 4.5%, unemployment was 10.8% and industrial output was 6.3% below its level a year earlier. Later vintages show these paths clearly. They do not separate weaker demand, oil prices, changes in expectations or the Fed’s independent contribution.
test: Would an equally persistent shift in expected inflation have occurred with less unemployment under a different policy? Survey forecasts, wage contracts and real borrowing rates around separate announcements would help distinguish expectations from the effects of the recession. A subsequent fall in inflation alone cannot answer that counterfactual.

details.heading: What changed on 6 October
details.text: The Saturday announcement changed the way the Fed supplied reserves. The trading desk placed greater weight on the quantity of nonborrowed reserves available to banks and allowed the overnight funds rate to fluctuate more. The Board raised the discount rate from 11% to 12% and imposed an 8% marginal reserve requirement on increases in certain managed liabilities, a source of wholesale funding for banks. Volcker acknowledged that control over money growth would be imprecise even from month to month. The announcement therefore provides a date for a change in policy practice. It supplies no single funds-rate increase that can represent the whole intervention. The Iranian oil disruption was already affecting costs, and precautionary oil demand could also raise prices. Treating every increase in energy prices as a supply loss would overstate that channel.

details.heading: Two contractions with a recovery between them
details.text: The March 1980 policy record documents another intervention. As part of President Carter’s anti-inflation programme, the Board announced voluntary credit restraint and required lenders to place special deposits equal to 15% of increases in certain consumer credit. That introduced a separate obstacle to financing purchases. In the revised monthly series, industrial production in July 1980 was 6.2% below the previous July and unemployment was 7.8%. By July 1981 production was 6.5% above its depressed year-earlier level. Its index, however, was still just below October 1979. The second contraction then pushed unemployment to 10.8% in November 1982. The Fed’s historical account identifies concentrated job losses in manufacturing, autos and construction. A comparison of the October 1979 and November 1982 endpoints misses the intervening recovery and the different exposure of those sectors to credit costs.

details.heading: How to distinguish the sources of disinflation
details.text: A rise in oil prices can squeeze household purchasing power and lift the price of energy-intensive goods. A persistent tightening of credit should also weaken demand for purchases that require financing, including housing and vehicles. A third mechanism is a change in the inflation rates people build into wages and contracts. To discriminate among them, align the October policy announcement and the subsequent credit restrictions with dated survey forecasts, wage settlements, housing permits and auto orders. Compare energy-intensive industries with less energy-intensive ones and classify their dependence on borrowing before the shock. A sustained fall in longer-horizon inflation forecasts ahead of widespread layoffs would support an expectations channel. Weakness concentrated first in financed purchases would support a credit channel. Use the statistics available on each observation date for that timing test. The chart’s revised industrial and labour series describe the eventual path.

name: From the technology slowdown to housing stress
headline: The same training window contains two different credit cycles
analysis: In January 2001 the FOMC cut its funds target as sales and production weakened. It still saw favourable longer-run productivity prospects. The late part of the decade had a different transmission channel. Housing activity peaked, losses on mortgage exposures strained institutions and disrupted funding. A model fitted through December 2008 includes part of that financial crisis. A sample ending in 2007 already includes the onset of market stress, although it excludes the most acute phase in autumn 2008.
test: Keep 2008 as a separate sensitivity check. For a technology or capital-spending slowdown, examine corporate orders, inventories and profits. For a housing-credit shock, examine collateral, mortgage performance, leverage and funding maturity. Similar GDP growth can conceal very different portfolio risks.

details.heading: Orders and investment in 2001
details.text: On 3 January 2001 the FOMC cut its funds target by half a percentage point to 6%. Its statement cited weakening sales and production, falling consumer confidence and high energy costs that squeezed purchasing power. It also reported continuing gains from technology and productivity. Firms can cut orders for new equipment because customers have slowed their spending even when that equipment remains productive. The two propositions have different implications for an investment recovery. The revised monthly series put industrial production 5.0% below its year-earlier level in November 2001 and unemployment at 5.5%, up from 3.9% in December 2000. Those outcomes were still in the future at the January meeting. A forecast made then could have tested the demand explanation against incoming orders, inventories and sales before assuming a deterioration in productive capacity.

details.heading: Credit supply and the demand to borrow
details.text: In the October 2007 lending survey, domestic banks reported tighter standards across prime, nontraditional and subprime mortgages while demand for mortgages also weakened. A fall in originations would therefore combine tighter access and fewer willing borrowers. By December 2007 revised industrial output was still 2.2% above its year-earlier level, with unemployment at 5.0%. Annual output growth had turned negative by June 2008. On 16 September the FOMC held its funds target at 2%. On 7 October the Board announced a facility to finance purchases of eligible three-month commercial paper, addressing borrowers’ ability to refinance short-term debt. About 85% of domestic respondents to the October survey reported tightening standards for large and middle-market business borrowers, up from about 60% in July. Large banks also reported more use of pre-existing credit lines. Loan balances could rise while access to new commitments deteriorated.

details.heading: What September’s industrial collapse can tell us
details.text: The Fed’s 16 October release initially put September production 2.8% below August and 4.5% below the previous September. It estimated that hurricanes accounted for about 2¼ percentage points of the monthly fall and the commercial-aircraft strike for another half point. The revised series now puts the annual decline at 8.1%. September’s aggregate alone is a poor measure of the contraction caused by financial stress. By December, industrial output stood 11.3% below a year earlier and unemployment had risen to 7.3%. For a test of credit transmission, compare order books and payrolls at firms with similar sales exposure but different pre-crisis dependence on wholesale financing. Separate new loan commitments from draws on old ones and exclude temporarily closed plants as a sensitivity check. Use each initial production release when reconstructing contemporary forecasts. Refit the historical comparison ending in 2007, then add 2008 to measure what the crisis months contribute.

name: The financial crisis
headline: Credit losses became a funding problem before unemployment peaked
analysis: As mortgage losses impaired financial balance sheets, borrowers and intermediaries faced a simultaneous fall in collateral values and loss of funding. By June 2009 US industrial production was 15.3% below its level a year earlier. Unemployment stood at 9.5% and reached 10.0% that October, after the business-cycle trough. Once the policy rate reached its lower bound, balance-sheet actions and the prospective path of rates became particularly important to financial pricing.
test: Distinguish losses that reduce net worth from a shortage of cash against sound collateral. Track market funding and loan conditions alongside the funds rate, and distinguish the month of the activity trough from the later peak in unemployment.

Federal Reserve Board · Term Securities Lending Facility

details.heading: Before Lehman, the mix of credit changed first
details.text: From 8 August 2007 to 10 September 2008, Reserve Bank credit grew by $55.6bn. Over the same interval the Fed’s outright securities holdings fell by $311.0bn, from 93% to 53% of Reserve Bank credit. By March 2008, banks had already borrowed $80bn through the Term Auction Facility. This change in the mix of the Fed’s claims matters for a lender assessing whether a borrower can roll its funding. The headline stock of central bank credit reveals little about which institutions could borrow, against what collateral, or for how long.

details.heading: Five weeks of expansion
details.text: Between 10 September and 15 October 2008, Reserve Bank credit rose by $846.8bn, while outright holdings rose by $10.9bn. Term auction credit increased by $113.1bn, only part of the expansion. The term auction provided funding to depository institutions against collateral. Under the separate Term Securities Lending Facility, primary dealers could borrow Treasuries against other eligible securities, improving the collateral available for private funding. The securities-for-securities exchange would be missed by counting outright purchases alone. The weekly stocks establish the change in scale and instrument mix. They leave open how much private funding would have disappeared without the facilities and whether the ultimate borrowers were solvent.

name: The pandemic and the credit backstop
headline: Market-functioning measures and income support worked through different channels
analysis: US unemployment rose from 3.5% in February 2020 to 14.8% in April. Industrial production was 17.3% below the previous April. A health shock closed or constrained businesses across sectors. The Fed’s 23 March measures supported securities market functioning and credit availability. Lending support could keep otherwise viable firms funded while revenues were interrupted. Household transfers and other fiscal programmes affected disposable income through a different channel. Combining every intervention under one measure of stimulus loses this distinction.
test: Compare spreads, volumes and funding access around facility announcements with spending after fiscal disbursements. The speed of employment loss makes the usual unemployment–inflation relationship from a conventional downturn a particularly fragile forecast guide.

name: Inflation after reopening
headline: A price shock met a different operating regime
analysis: When the FOMC raised rates on June 15, 2022, the latest published U.S. headline CPI reading was May’s 8.6% year-on-year increase. The Committee cited pandemic-related imbalances, energy costs and broader price pressures, and anticipated further increases. June’s 9.1% headline reading arrived on July 13. The chart calculates year-on-year inflation from the seasonally adjusted index, yielding about 9.0% for June, when unemployment was 3.6%. The energy shock invites a comparison with the 1970s. In 2022, however, administered rates in an ample-reserves system carried the policy signal that the Fed had sought to convey through its reserve operations in October 1979.
test: Separate the instrument from the economic shock. The inflation test below compares the same predictors across several training periods. For market pricing, compare changes in expected future rates and longer yields around the same announcement, rather than mapping the size of a rate change directly onto the bond return.
